caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Belgium has one of Western Europe's highest debt stocks: 91.5% of GDP in 2006, a low of 87.3% in 2007, then climbing through the crisis to 111.2% in 2020, the series peak. Post-COVID consolidation and growth brought it to 103.1% in 2022, but the trend has turned up again to a projected 106.3% in 2025 as fiscal consolidation stalled. GDP rose from $408.3bn in 2006 to a projected $724.9bn in 2025. Borrowing costs remain low as a euro-area core issuer, but the upward debt drift is a genuine policy concern.
inflation_management: Belgium's inflation follows the ECB cycle with a domestic twist: automatic wage indexation amplifies imported shocks into persistent price growth. It was 0% in 2009 and 0.4% in 2020, then surged to 10.3% in 2022, the series high, on energy prices — and indexation pushed it to 4.3% in 2024 even as the euro-area average fell faster; it is projected at 3.0% for 2025. The ECB's policy is the instrument; Belgium's wage-setting institutions determine the domestic echo.

key_events.event: Financial crisis and eurozone turmoil; bank rescues (Fortis, Dexia) permanently raised the debt stock.
COVID-19: debt hit 111.2% of GDP, the series peak, on pandemic spending and contraction.
Energy crisis drove inflation to 10.3%; automatic wage indexation kept it elevated into 2024.
Federal elections (June 2024) ushered in a long government-formation process amid fiscal consolidation pressure.
Debt projected at 106.3% of GDP as consolidation efforts continued to lag targets.

outlook_next_decade: The central fiscal question is whether Belgium can resume a credible downward debt path from above 100% of GDP. Inflation should converge toward the ECB target as the indexation echo fades, supporting real-income recovery. Structural issues are slow growth, aging-related spending pressure, and a complex federal governance structure that slows fiscal adjustment. Debt remains sustainable at current rates, but the margin for complacency is thin if European rate cycles turn.
